title: Progressive Reveal Matrix: Micro-presets for Hybrid Prefetching & Batch Guardrails
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Goal:
Design a compact, progressive-disclosure UI component (Progressive Reveal Matrix) for Redwood Console that helps operators choose ‘micro-presets’ for hybrid prefetching and batching. The component must surface the tradeoffs between token cost, tail-latency, and cache hit-rate, provide transparent explainers for each preset, and include guardrails and an undoable rollout playground. This is meant to sit on the Route -> Optimize tab alongside existing batching recommendations but as a more lightweight, scenario-driven entry point for operators who are unfamiliar with raw knobs.

Key user problems to solve:
- Engineers/DevOps want a quick, low-risk way to reduce token spend without surprising latency regressions.
- Product/platform leads need explainable choices to present to stakeholders (cost vs availability).
- On-call and SRE need safe rollback and audit trails when toggling prefetch/batch behaviors.

Scope / deliverables:
- A responsive UI card (compact + expanded states) showing 3 curated micro-presets (Conservative, Balanced, Aggressive) plus a custom slider mode.
- A small matrix visualization mapping presets to projected 95th-ms latency delta, estimated token savings, and expected cache hit-rate. Values show a confidence band and an explanatory tooltip.
- Inline micro-copy that explains what changes (e.g., prefetch depth, prefix caching TTL, batch window ms) and the runtime features required.
- A Guardrails panel with automated safety checks (max latency delta, minimum hit-rate), a suggested canary rollout schedule, and a one-click rollback playbook that links to the rollout timeline.
- An interactive simulation mode that runs a lightweight scenario (sample trace) and animates expected outcomes. Simulation should clearly label assumptions and a calibrated confidence band.

Acceptance criteria:
- Design files in Figma for compact/expanded card and simulation animation (desktop + tablet).
- Annotated Handoff doc detailing component states, telemetry events to emit, and fallback UX when runtime does not support prefetch.
- Usability script for a 5-minute moderated test with internal ops users.
- List of engineering risks and required runtime hooks (KV cache TTL control, prefetch depth parameter, batch window override).

Design decisions and tradeoffs considered:
- Show 3 curated presets rather than exposing raw knobs to lower cognitive load; provide a custom mode for advanced users.
- Use confidence bands instead of single-point estimates to communicate uncertainty in cost/latency projections.
- Keep the simulation lightweight; heavy simulations deferred to a separate playground to avoid blocking rollout.

Handoff artifacts and links:
- Figma prototype (compact -> expanded -> simulation): https://figma.com/file/abc123/progressive-reveal-matrix
- Handoff confluence page / PRD: https://confluence.redwood-inference.com/display/OPS/Progressive+Reveal+Matrix
- Prototype recording (mp4) demonstrating simulation and rollback: https://drive.redwood-inference.com/drive/folders/PRJ-ops-prototypes/PRM-sim-2026-02-28.mp4
- Suggested telemetry events (string list included in handoff doc): preset_selected, preset_previewed, simulation_started, rollout_initiated, rollback_executed

Open questions for engineering:
- Can the runtime provide estimated token savings per preset by sampling recent traces, or must we use static heuristics?
- What is the minimum telemetry/trace retention required to compute a meaningful confidence band?
- Are partial-rollouts by customer tier supported in Dedicated/Private today or do we fall back to region-only rollouts?

Next steps:
1) Sync with Arjun (serving runtime) and Sophie (PM) to validate runtime hooks and telemetry.
2) Run quick internal usability test with Platform and SRE (using the 5-minute script).
3) Iterate Figma based on feedback and produce annotated handoff (events + CSS tokens).

Notes on uniqueness / design rationale:
This pattern intentionally emphasizes progressive disclosure (compact card first) and scenario-driven explainers to ease adoption. It complements existing full-featured Config Labs by acting as a low-friction entry point that surfaces recommended safe defaults and an audit-ready rollback path.
